headline: Microsoft Retires Its Friendly AI Character 'Mico' From Copilot's Voice Chat

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Microsoft makes a computer helper called Copilot. Copilot can talk to you using your voice, like a friend. Last year, Microsoft added a cute yellow blob character named Mico. Mico had a face and would smile, react, and show feelings while you talked to it. Now Microsoft says Mico will not show up when you use Copilot's voice chat anymore. Instead, Mico will move to a different part of Microsoft called Learn Live, which is used for learning things. Microsoft says Mico taught them a lot about how people like talking to computers in a warm and friendly way. This is not the first helper Microsoft has removed. Long ago they had a paperclip helper named Clippy, and other helpers named Cortana and Rover, that they also stopped using. Microsoft is changing Copilot because they want to combine two of their apps into one bigger app. This shows that even fun computer characters can disappear when companies decide to change their plans.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Microsoft has an AI chatbot called Copilot, which can have voice conversations with people. About a year ago, Microsoft added a friendly yellow blob character named Mico to make talking with Copilot feel more personal. Mico would react with facial expressions and animations while listening to what you said, kind of like a digital face for the AI. Now Microsoft has announced that Mico will no longer appear during Copilot's voice conversations. Instead, the character will move to Learn Live, a Microsoft platform focused on education, where Microsoft says Mico will have 'more to react to.' This change is happening gradually, in stages, rather than all at once. Microsoft explained that Mico helped the company understand how people want AI to sound and feel, and that this knowledge will still shape how Copilot works in the future, even without the character being visible. This isn't the first time Microsoft has retired a virtual assistant. Older examples include Clippy, the paperclip helper from Microsoft Word, along with Cortana and Rover. The removal of Mico is part of a bigger plan to combine two separate Microsoft apps, the regular Copilot app and Microsoft 365 Copilot, into a single app. It also follows a leadership change where a new executive, Jacob Andreou, took charge of Copilot, while the AI chief who created Mico moved on to focus on building new AI models instead.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Microsoft's AI assistant, Copilot, is losing one of its most recognizable features: an animated yellow blob character named Mico. Mico was introduced less than a year ago as part of Copilot's voice mode, the feature that lets people talk to the AI out loud instead of typing. Mico would react in real time with facial expressions and animations, giving Copilot a sense of personality. Microsoft's own AI leader had described the character as a way to give the chatbot an 'identity' that felt more relatable than plain text or a robotic voice. Now, according to a Microsoft support page, Mico will be pulled from Copilot's voice mode and moved instead to Learn Live, a Microsoft platform built for education, where the company says the character will have 'more to react to.' The rollout of this change is happening in waves rather than all at once, meaning some users may notice it before others. Microsoft explained the decision by saying that Mico taught the company valuable lessons about warmth, expressiveness, and how people actually want to interact with AI, and that these lessons will continue shaping Copilot even without Mico's face attached to it. This isn't an isolated event. Microsoft has a long history of introducing friendly virtual assistants and later shutting them down, including Clippy, the paperclip character from early versions of Microsoft Word, as well as Cortana and Rover. The removal of Mico is also connected to bigger changes happening behind the scenes at Microsoft. The company is working to merge its two separate Copilot apps, one built for general consumers and one built for Microsoft 365 productivity tools, into a single unified app. This shift comes only months after Microsoft reorganized its AI leadership, putting a new executive, Jacob Andreou, in charge of Copilot, while Mustafa Suleyman, the AI chief who introduced Mico, shifted his focus toward developing new AI models. Together, these changes suggest Microsoft is rethinking not just how Copilot looks, but how the entire product is organized and who leads its direction.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Microsoft is discontinuing Mico, the animated yellow blob character that has represented its Copilot AI assistant's voice mode since its debut less than a year ago. Voice mode allows users to speak with Copilot rather than typing, and Mico was designed to make that experience feel warmer by displaying facial expressions and reactive animations as the conversation unfolded. When Mico launched, Microsoft's AI chief, Mustafa Suleyman, framed the character as a way to give the chatbot a distinct 'identity,' something that could make an AI feel more approachable rather than purely functional. According to a Microsoft support page, Mico is now being phased out of Copilot's voice mode 'in waves,' meaning the change will roll out gradually rather than instantly for every user. Instead of disappearing entirely, Mico will be relocated to Learn Live, a Microsoft platform focused on education, where the company claims the character will have 'more to react to' in learning-based interactions. Microsoft framed the decision not as a failure but as a natural evolution, stating that Mico helped the company understand concepts like warmth and expressiveness in AI conversation, insights that will continue to inform Copilot's design even without a visible mascot. This retirement fits into a long pattern at Microsoft, which has introduced and later abandoned several virtual assistants over the decades, including Clippy, the paperclip character once embedded in Microsoft Office; Cortana, its voice assistant that competed with products like Siri and Alexa; and Rover, a lesser-known animated helper. What makes Mico's removal notable is the surrounding context. The change is tied to Microsoft's broader plan to merge two separate products, the consumer-facing Copilot app and Microsoft 365 Copilot, which is built into workplace tools, into one unified application. Simplifying the product lineup could make Copilot easier to manage and market, but it also means visual branding choices like Mico may not survive the transition if they don't fit the merged product's direction. Additionally, this shift comes only months after a leadership reorganization in which Jacob Andreou was placed in charge of Copilot, while Suleyman, the executive who championed Mico's launch, redirected his attention toward developing new underlying AI models rather than the consumer-facing app. This suggests that decisions about Copilot's future may increasingly prioritize the technology's core capabilities and business strategy over cultivating a friendly on-screen character, even one that had only recently been introduced as central to the assistant's personality.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Microsoft is retiring Mico, the expressive yellow blob character that has served as the visual face of Copilot's voice mode since its introduction less than a year ago. Voice mode lets users speak with the AI assistant conversationally rather than typing, and Mico was built to enhance that experience by reacting in real time with facial expressions and animations, giving the interaction a sense of personality and presence. At launch, Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman positioned Mico as an intentional branding choice, arguing that an AI chatbot benefits from having a distinct 'identity' rather than existing as a faceless, text-based tool. According to a company support page, Microsoft will now phase Mico out of Copilot's voice mode 'in waves,' a gradual rollout that suggests the company is testing or managing the transition carefully rather than removing the feature abruptly for all users simultaneously. Rather than eliminating the character altogether, Microsoft is relocating Mico to Learn Live, an educational platform, where the company states the avatar will have 'more to react to,' implying that structured learning content offers richer material for an expressive character than open-ended conversation does. In its official statement, Microsoft characterized the decision as a natural extension of experimentation rather than an admission of failure, noting that Mico provided valuable insight into warmth, expressiveness, and how users want to engage with conversational AI, lessons the company says will continue to shape Copilot's design going forward. This retirement continues a recognizable pattern in Microsoft's history of launching, and later discontinuing, anthropomorphized digital assistants intended to make software feel more human. Predecessors include Clippy, the paperclip character once built into Microsoft Office to offer writing tips; Cortana, the voice assistant that once competed directly with Apple's Siri and Amazon's Alexa; and Rover, a lesser-known animated search assistant. What distinguishes Mico's removal from these earlier cases is the broader strategic context surrounding it. Microsoft is currently working to consolidate its Copilot ecosystem by merging the general-purpose Copilot app with Microsoft 365 Copilot, the version integrated into workplace productivity tools like Word and Outlook, into a single unified application. Streamlining separate products into one experience often requires eliminating features or design elements that don't align cleanly across both use cases, and a mascot designed primarily for casual voice interaction may not translate well into a productivity-focused environment. Compounding this, the change follows a recent leadership reshuffling in which Jacob Andreou was installed to oversee Copilot, while Suleyman, the executive who had championed Mico as central to Copilot's identity, shifted his focus toward developing Microsoft's underlying AI models rather than consumer-facing product design. Taken together, these developments suggest that Copilot's future direction may be shaped more by technical capability, unified product strategy, and business priorities than by cultivating a distinct, character-driven personality for the AI.

questions: Why do you think companies like Microsoft create friendly characters like Mico or Clippy to represent their technology, and do you think it actually changes how comfortable people feel using AI?
If you used an AI assistant every day at school, would you want it to have a visual character with expressions, or would you rather it just be a voice or text? Why?

Microsoft has created and then removed several virtual helpers over the years. What does this pattern suggest about how technology companies test new ideas, and how might that affect the tools you use in the future?
